node.label: Ernest Gellner
node.date_label: Thought and Change (1964) · Nations and Nationalism (1983) · Encounters with Nationalism (1994) · Warwick reply, “Do nations have navels?” (1995)
node.description: Relates nationalism to the mobility, specialized work and expensive shared literate culture of modern societies. In his Warwick reply, cultural continuity is possible but contingent rather than necessary to national formation. He accepts that preindustrial cultures could be consciously valued and sometimes politically expressed; this qualification complicates a simple claim that the past never matters. Anthony D. Smith’s opening challenges the sufficiency of a general modernist account for particular nationalisms. Their disagreement concerns explanatory weight and historical specificity, not a settled opposition between an ahistorical modernism and an unchanging ethnic essence.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Thought and Change (1964); Nations and Nationalism (1983); Encounters with Nationalism (1994); Warwick reply (delivered 1995; published 1996).

proposed_edges.relationship: Links nationalism to modern mobility and mastery of a shared literate culture maintained through political and educational institutions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Retained primary Gellner reply, with newly inspected central paragraphs on mobility/high culture and contingent continuities. These are his explanatory claims, not a universal outcome or an assertion that cultures lacked any earlier political expression.

proposed_edges.relationship: Contests the explanatory necessity of premodern cultural continuity while acknowledging that such continuity sometimes exists.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Direct named Warwick reply to Smith’s opening; both are primary debate statements. Gellner’s provocative primordialist label is not adopted as Smith’s self-definition; Gellner explicitly concedes contingent continuities. No collective nationalism-field arrow is changed.
